'''Helen Thom Edwards''' (May 27, 1936 – June 21, 2016) was an American [[physicist]].<ref name=":0">{{cite web|url=https://www.macfound.org/fellows/332/|title=Helen T. Edwards — MacArthur Foundation|work=macfound.org|access-date=4 November 2016}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |date=2016-05-27 |title=Helen Edwards |url=https://pubs.aip.org/physicstoday/online/8949/Helen-Edwards |journal=Physics Today |language=English |doi=10.1063/PT.5.031231|url-access=subscription }}</ref> She is best known for her role as the lead scientist in the design and construction of the [[Tevatron]] at the [[Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory]],<ref>{{Cite web |title=Fermilab {{!}} Tevatron {{!}} Shutdown Process |url=https://www.fnal.gov/pub/tevatron/shutdown-process.html |access-date=2025-03-15 |website=www.fnal.gov}}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite web |last=Hesla |first=Leah |last2=Salles |first2=Andre |date=2016-06-27 |title=Helen Edwards, visionary behind Fermilab's Tevatron, dies |url=https://news.fnal.gov/2016/06/helen-edwards-visionary-behind-fermilabs-tevatron-dies/ |access-date=2025-03-15 |website=News |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name=":3">{{cite web |title=DESY mourns Helen Edwards |url=http://www.desy.de/news/news_search/index_eng.html?openDirectAnchor=1066&two_columns=0 |access-date=1 May 2019 |website=DESY}}</ref> which was the most powerful [[Collider|particle collider]] in the world until 2009.<ref name=":2" />

== Early life and education ==
Helen Thom was born on May 27, 1936, in Detroit, Michigan<ref name=":1" /> to Mary Milner Thom and Edgar Robertson Thom.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Helen Thom Edwards - Ancestry® |url=https://www.ancestry.com/genealogy/records/helen-thom-edwards-24-1dgrx41 |access-date=2025-03-15 |website=www.ancestry.com |language=en-US}}</ref> The youngest of five siblings, Helen spent much of her early life in [[Pontiac, Michigan]] until her family moved to a ranch in [[Metamora, Illinois|Metamora]], Michigan.<ref name=":4">{{Cite book |last=Stephens |first=Nastassja |url=https://bpb-us-e1.wpmucdn.com/blog.umd.edu/dist/e/952/files/2021/05/HelenEdwards.pdf |title=The Life and Legacy of Helen Thom Edwards |date=May 17, 2020 |publisher=University of Maryland |format=PDF}}</ref> Thom attended the Kingswood School (now the [[Cranbrook Schools#:~:text=Kingswood School Cranbrook (for girls,Brookside School Cranbrook in 1930.|Cranbrook Schools]]) in [[Bloomfield Hills, Michigan]] until 1950, when she transferred to [[Madeira School|The Madeira School]] in [[McLean, Virginia]].<ref name=":4" /> At Madeira, Thom served as vice-head of student government and fire chief, while also participating in varsity hockey, basketball, and horseback riding.<ref name=":4" /> Thom's struggles with [[dyslexia]], a learning disorder that was widely misunderstood at the time, led her parents to believe that she was not very bright.<ref name=":5">{{Cite web |title=The Quest for Everything |url=https://www.lostwomenofscience.org/podcast-episodes/the-quest-for-everything#transcript |access-date=2025-03-15 |website=www.lostwomenofscience.org |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":4" /> However, despite her distaste for reading and writing,<ref name=":5" /> Thom excelled in mathematics and science.<ref name=":4" />

After graduating from [[The Madeira School]] in 1953,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Madeira Alumnae {{!}} The Madeira School |url=https://www.madeira.org/community/madeira-alums/madeira-alumnae |access-date=2025-03-15 |website=www.madeira.org |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Helen T. Edwards {{!}} SNF |url=https://snf.ieeecsc.org/contact/helen-t-edwards#memoriam |access-date=2025-03-15 |website=snf.ieeecsc.org}}</ref> Thom pursued her undergraduate studies at [[Cornell University]], where she earned a B.S. in physics in 1957.<ref name=":0" /> She remained at Cornell to continue her education, working with [[cosmic ray]] specialist [[Kenneth Greisen]] on the development of [[Air shower (physics)|electromagnetic showers]]. Helen met her husband, Donald Edwards, while working at the Laboratory of Nuclear Studies during her masters; they married in 1963, the same year she completed her M.S. in physics. Edwards subsequently began<ref name=":6">{{Cite web |title=Prominent researchers, both Cornell alumni, endow accelerator physics chair, the Boyce McDaniel Professorship, at Cornell {{!}} Cornell Chronicle |url=https://news.cornell.edu/stories/2001/01/alumni-endow-boyce-mcdaniel-accelerator-physics-professorship |access-date=2025-03-15 |website=news.cornell.edu |language=en}}</ref> her doctoral studies under [[Boyce McDaniel]] in the Laboratory of Nuclear Studies at Cornell University.<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://nap.nationalacademies.org/read/11172/chapter/10 |title=Read "Biographical Memoirs: Volume 85" at NAP.edu |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":4" /> In 1966, at the age of 30, Edwards completed her Ph.D. in [[Experimental physics|Experimental Physics]].<ref name=":6" /><ref name=":4" />

==Research and career==
After earning her Ph.D, Edwards continued her work in the Laboratory of Nuclear Studies at Cornell University as a research associate.<ref name=":0" /> Working under [[Robert R. Wilson]], she contributed to the final stages of the 10 G[[Electronvolt|eV]] [[Synchrotron]] project<ref>{{cite journal |last=Mcdaniel |first=Boyce |author2=Albert Silverman |date=October 1968 |title=The 10‐GeV synchrotron at Cornell |journal=Physics Today |volume=21 |issue=10 |pages=29–38 |bibcode=1968PhT....21j..29M |doi=10.1063/1.3034533}}</ref><ref name=":7">{{Cite web |date=2022-07-26 |title=Helen Edwards: pioneer of Fermilab's Tevatron |url=https://physicsworld.com/a/helen-edwards-pioneer-of-the-tevatron/ |access-date=2024-01-12 |website=Physics World |language=en-GB}}</ref> helping to develop the "resonant beam extraction" technique, which enabled physicists to extract high-energy [[Particle beam|beams]] from [[Particle accelerator|circular accelerators]].<ref name=":7" /> In 1967, the first [[particle beam]] circulated in the [[Synchrotron]], and by March 1968, the accelerated reached its full energy potential of 10 GeV, the highest recorded for an electron synchrotron at the time.<ref name=":7" />

That same year, Wilson, who had become the founding director of the National Laboratory (later renamed [[Fermilab|Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory]], or Fermilab), invited both Helen Edwards and her husband, Donald Edwards, to join him at the institution. In 1970, Helen was appointed Associate Head of the Booster Section by Wilson,<ref name=":7" /> where she initially worked to build the lab's 8 GeV Booster. The accelerator successfully launched its first beam at 7 GeV in June 1971, and reached its full potential of 200 GeV by March 1972.<ref name=":4" />
Edwards's most significant contribution was her leadership in the design, construction, and operation of the [[Tevatron]], which was the world's first successful [[Superconductivity|superconducting]] [[synchrotron]]<ref name=":8">{{Cite web |date=2010-12-28 |title=LAWRENCE Helen T. Edwards, 1986 {{!}} U.S. DOE Office of Science (SC) |url=https://science.osti.gov/lawrence/Award-Laureates/1980s/edwards |access-date=2025-03-15 |website=science.osti.gov |language=en-US}}</ref> and the most powerful particle collider in the world for 26 years.<ref name=":7" /> The Tevatron was built directly beneath the Main Ring at Fermilab and boasted a circumference of about 6.5&nbsp;km,<ref name=":7" /> or 4 miles.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Higgins |first=Valerie |date=2021-03-08 |title=A brief history of women of Fermilab |url=https://news.fnal.gov/2021/03/a-brief-history-of-women-of-fermilab/ |access-date=2025-03-15 |website=News |language=en-US}}</ref> Using superconducting magnets to accelerate [[proton]]s and [[antiproton]]s at 1 trillion electron volts (TeV),<ref name=":9">"Helen T. Edwards." ''Notable Women Scientists'', Gale, 2009. ''Gale In Context: Biography'', link.gale.com/apps/doc/K1668000111/BIC?u=columbiau&sid=summon&xid=5bbd1685. Accessed 15 Mar. 2025.</ref> particles could reach 99.999954% of the speed of light.<ref name=":7" /> Traveling at such high speeds, particles collided at about 2 TeV to create energy levels similar to those of the [[atom]]s from a fraction of a second after the [[Big Bang]].<ref name=":9" /> As hypothesized by the [[Standard Model]], these collisions would provide insight into the simplest building block of matter: the interior of atoms themselves.<ref name=":5" /><ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-02-23 |title=Building Blocks - NASA Science |url=https://science.nasa.gov/universe/overview/building-blocks/ |access-date=2025-03-15 |language=en-US}}</ref>

On July 5, 1979, the [[United States Department of Energy|US Department of Energy]] authorized the Tevatron's construction,<ref name=":10">{{Cite web |last= |date=2011-09-30 |title=Tevatron shuts down, but analysis continues |url=https://news.fnal.gov/2011/09/tevatron-shuts-analysis-continues/ |access-date=2025-03-15 |website=News |language=en-US}}</ref> and  [[Leon M. Lederman]], Fermilab's second director, placed Edwards in charge of the project.<ref name=":4" /> Among her significant contributions to the design and implementation of the Tevatron, she developed a system that enabled the Tevatron to detect [[antiproton]]s and [[proton]]s from different sources nearly simultaneously.<ref name=":9" /> According to Paul Czarapata, an engineer who worked at Fermilab alongside Edwards, "[Helen] was behind everything that happened every day. Sometimes I wondered if she lived there 24 hours a day."<ref name=":5" />
On March 18, 1983, the final magnet was installed on the Tevatron, creating a total of 774 [[superconducting magnet]]s.<ref name=":10" /> Each magnet contained over 20 miles of superconducting wire in the [[Rutherford cable]] form; in total, Fermilab is estimated to have purchased 95% of the [[Niobium–titanium|niobium-titanium]] ever produced in human history.<ref name=":5" /> In July 1983, the machine fired its first particles, reaching a world-record energy of 512 GeV.<ref name=":11">{{Cite web |last=Wisniewski |first=Rhianna |date=2012-02-01 |title=The Tevatron's proud legacy {{!}} symmetry magazine |url=https://www.symmetrymagazine.org/article/february-2012/tevatrons-proud-legacy?language_content_entity=und |access-date=2025-03-15 |website=www.symmetrymagazine.org |language=en}}</ref> Physicist Dmitri Denisov, who helped update the Tevatron, notes that "The Tevatron is the [[particle physics]] equivalent of landing on the moon. We achieved something that, scientifically and technically, wasn't possible before."<ref name=":11" />
The Tevatron recorded its first [[Annihilation|proton-antiproton collisions]] in 1985 and was used to find the [[top quark]] in 1995 and the [[tau neutrino]] in 2000.<ref name=":7" /> Using the mass of the [[top quark]] from the Tevatron, physicists were able to calculate the [[mass]] of the crucial [[Higgs boson]].<ref name=":7" />

In 1987, Edwards became head of the Accelerator Division, continuing to lead the research on the Tevatron.<ref name=":0" /> Between 1989 and 1991, she served as Technical Director of the 54-mile [[Superconducting Super Collider]] in Texas, which aimed to create collisions at 40 TeV.<ref name=":7" /><ref name=":2" /><ref name=":9" /> However, the project fell short due to funding cuts.<ref name=":9" />
After 1992, Edwards continued her work at Fermilab as a guest scientist, where she made significant contributions to the development of high-[[gradient]], superconducting [[Linear particle accelerator|linear accelerators]] as well as bright, intense electron sources. She collaborated with scientists at [[DESY]] in [[Hamburg|Hamburg, Germany]] to develop the [[International Linear Collider#Merging of regional proposals into a worldwide project|TESLA superconducting linear collider]] and the [[photoinjector]] for the TESLA Test Facility ([[FLASH]]).<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":3" />

In September 2011, the Tevatron was shut down, marking the end of its groundbreaking contributions to particle physics. Edwards, wearing a cowboy hat in homage to the nickname for the Accelerator Division team, pushed the button to halt its operations.<ref name=":7" />

== Positions ==

* 1966-70 Research Associate, 10 GEV Electron Synchrotron, Cornell University
* 1970-87 Associate Head of the Booster Group, Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory
* 1987-89 Head, Accelerator Division, Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory
* 1988 MacArthur Fellow
* 1989-92 Head & Associate Director, Superconducting Division, [[Superconducting Super Collider]] Laboratory, Dallas
* 1992–2010 Guest scientist, Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory

Wilson Prize from the American Physical Society |url=https://news.fnal.gov/2002/10/fermilabs-helen-edwards-receives-prestigious-2003-robert-r-wilson-prize-american-physical-society/ |access-date=2025-03-15 |website=News |language=en-US}}</ref>

Six years after Edwards's death, a bill was introduced in the [[United States Senate|US Senate]] and [[United States House of Representatives|US House of Representatives]] in 2022 to rename Fermilab's Integrated Engineering Research Center in honor of the late Helen Edwards.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-02-03 |title=Foster, Durbin, Duckworth Introduce Resolution to Name Fermilab Research Center After Renowned Physicist Dr. Helen Edwards {{!}} Congressman Bill Foster |url=https://foster.house.gov/media/press-releases/foster-durbin-duckworth-introduce-resolution-name-fermilab-research-center |access-date=2025-03-15 |website=foster.house.gov |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Legislators hope to rename center after particle physicist Edwards - South Southwest |url=https://digitaledition.chicagotribune.com/tribune/article_popover.aspx?guid=6aaaeb9f-a406-473c-a745-397e1e758e05 |access-date=2025-03-15 |website=digitaledition.chicagotribune.com}}</ref> Additionally, Fermilab established the Helen Edwards Summer Internship, which provides students studying physics and engineering in Europe with the opportunity to work with scientists at Fermilab.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Internships for International Students Studying out of Country {{!}} Internships |url=https://internships.fnal.gov/internships-for-international-students-studying-out-of-country/ |access-date=2025-03-15 |language=en-US}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Helen met Donald Edwards, a doctoral student at [[Cornell University|Cornell]], while working in the Laboratory of Nuclear Studies during her master's program.<ref name=":4" /> The couple married in 1963 and collaborated on numerous projects throughout their careers,<ref name=":4" /> including their work at Fermilab.<ref>{{Cite web |date=March 19, 1970 |title=Helen Edwards is Associate Head of Booster Section |url=https://history.fnal.gov/historical/people/edwards_associate_head.html |access-date=2025-03-15 |website=history.fnal.gov}}</ref>

In 1992, Helen and Donald Edwards retired in [[Montana]],<ref name=":7" /><ref name=":2" /> where Helen, a lifelong nature lover, pursued her passion for photographing wildlife.<ref name=":7" /> Despite retiring, they continued contributing to the field as guest scientists at Fermilab until 2010.<ref name=":7" /><ref name=":2" />

In 2001, Helen and Donald demonstrated their enduring commitment to the advancement of the field by endowing a chair in [[accelerator physics]] at their alma mater, Cornell University.<ref name=":6" />
